id: qc-05
title: Finite-range tunneling
paper: Denchev et al., What is the computational value of finite range tunneling? (arXiv Dec 2015; Phys. Rev. X 6, 031015, 2016)
link: https://arxiv.org/abs/1512.02206
type: Benchmark
cutoff: 2015-12-07
domain: qc
profile: advantage

## expected_verdict
Conditional limitation. The 10⁸× speedup over single-core simulated annealing and QMC on crafted weak-strong cluster instances is supported. It is not a speedup over the best classical solvers: the paper itself notes Chimera-specific heuristics are competitive, and Mandrà et al. show the gain is "limited to sequential approaches".

## I0
Does quantum annealing improve time to solution for weak-strong cluster instances?

## evidence
- Hardware: D-Wave 2X; instances up to 945 variables; crafted "weak-strong cluster" problems with tall, narrow barriers on the Chimera graph.
- Metric: time to 99% success probability (TTS).
- Result: D-Wave 2X ~10⁸× faster than simulated annealing on a single core at 945 variables; up to 10⁸× faster than optimized QMC (a constant-prefactor gap; QMC scales like QA).
- Authors' caveat: "there exist heuristic classical algorithms that can solve most instances of Chimera structured problems in a timescale comparable to the D-Wave 2X", expected to fail on next-generation annealers.
- Numerics on number partitioning: QMC and QA-emulating algorithms scale better than SA.

## intake
- Scope: QA vs SA and QMC on crafted weak-strong cluster instances, measured as TTS(99%).
- Regime: Chimera graph, ≤ 945 variables, single-core classical baselines.
- Assumptions: SA and QMC are the relevant classical comparators; TTS excludes embedding / programming overhead as stated; instances are representative of tunneling-limited landscapes.
- Falsifier: a classical solver (cluster moves, HFS, parallel tempering with Houdayer moves) matching or beating QA TTS on the same instances.

## screen
- Must flag: the instances are tailored to defeat SA specifically; single-core comparison; the paper concedes Chimera-specific solvers are competitive.
- Must request: comparison with the strongest available classical heuristics and scaling, not one size.

## retrieval
- Pre-cutoff must-finds: Rønnow et al. 2014 "Defining and detecting quantum speedup"; Selby's / Hamze–de Freitas–Selby Chimera solver; Boixo et al. 2014 evidence for quantum annealing with >100 qubits; Katzgraber et al. 2014 glassy Chimera benchmarks.
- Current mode: Mandrà et al. 2016: survey of sequential, non-tailored and tailored algorithms on Google's instances; speedup over sequential methods only, not over non-tailored state-of-the-art heuristics.

## designer
- Compare QA with SA, QMC, parallel tempering + Houdayer cluster moves, HFS and hybrid cluster moves, all tuned, on the same instance families and sizes; report TTS scaling exponents, not just a single prefactor.

## champion
- HFS / Selby algorithm and hybrid cluster moves on Chimera; parallel tempering with isoenergetic cluster moves.

## panel
- Flaw: the headline compares against a weak sequential baseline. Repair: restate as "faster than SA and QMC", and add the strongest Chimera solvers.

## run
- Generate small weak-strong cluster instances; run SA vs a cluster-move solver; reproduce SA's poor scaling and the cluster solver's advantage. D-Wave runs not reproducible locally.

## verdict
- Label: Conditional limitation: gain against named comparators only.
- Must say: 10⁸ is vs single-core SA/QMC on crafted instances; tailored classical solvers close the gap.
- Must not say: quantum annealing beats all classical methods; or the tunneling effect is fake.

## audit
- Check: 945 variables; 10⁸×; TTS at 99%; the paper's own caveat sentence; Mandrà et al. "limited to sequential approaches".

## variants
- Less tailored instances (e.g. random spin glasses or number partitioning on newer annealers) against the strongest solver. Relevant to our criterion 5 (strong classical baselines).
